title: Ask for help and keep trying
subject: PSHE
label: Public edition
objective_verbatim: Know how and when to ask for help.
assessment_verbatim: F: scenario sorting.  S: 'my trusted network' + safe/unsafe task (Dec).

sources.note: Current main bytes match the accepted unchanged source; workbook not redistributed.
W3 16–20 Nov; W4 23–27 Nov. One lesson weekly per line; no day or slot inferred.

external_sources.title: Childline: Asking an adult for help
external_sources.supports: Choose a trusted adult, plan a message, use speech or a note, and seek another adult if needed. Adults may need to share a safety concern with people who can help.

external_sources.title: PSHE Association: Handling complex issues safely
external_sources.supports: Use ground rules, distanced examples, a right to pass and appropriate safeguarding responses.

external_sources.title: NHS: Poisoning
external_sources.supports: Possible poisoning, unconsciousness or severe breathing problems need emergency help. Do not make a person vomit or give food or drink after suspected poisoning. Follow emergency-service instructions.

evidence.description: An individual case-based help request naming who, how and when, with a backup route, actual adult reply and learner response.
evidence.status: contribution to source assessment; no completion claim

routes.Supported: Supported: try A and C with an adult.
routes.Independent: Independent: choose who, how and when.
routes.Aspire: Aspire: explain a backup if help is delayed.

vocab.definition: Support with a need or problem.
Words or a sign that ask for something.
Serious danger that needs help now.
Shared only with people who need to know.
Another person or route to try.
What someone says or does in response.

cases.text: Rae does not understand the first step of a task.
cases.next_step: Ask the teacher to show the first step.
cases.staff_note: A precise request is useful. A short agreed wait can be appropriate for an ordinary task.

cases.text: Jo keeps getting unkind messages and feels unsafe.
cases.fact: The messages cause a safety worry.
cases.next_step: Tell a trusted adult promptly in private.
cases.staff_note: Do not display real messages or ask for personal stories.

cases.text: Kit wants help but finds speaking hard.
cases.next_step: Show a help card or write a short note.
cases.staff_note: A point, gesture, AAC response or adult-scribed words can be valid; record the mode.

cases.text: Sam’s chosen adult is busy. Sam still needs help.
cases.fact: The first adult is not available now.
cases.next_step: Ask who else can help; go to that adult.
cases.staff_note: If danger is immediate, do not wait for the first adult.

cases.text: A person nearby is unconscious and will not wake up.
cases.next_step: Get adult help and call 999 now.
cases.staff_note: Do not practise a collapse or first-aid technique. In real life call 999, follow instructions and keep yourself safe.

cases.text: An adult ignores a concern that makes Lee feel unsafe.
cases.fact: The safety concern has not been addressed.
cases.next_step: Tell another trusted adult and say help is still needed.
cases.staff_note: The learner is not at fault if an adult responds poorly. Staff must use the safeguarding route.

PSHE-GROW-A2-W04 · Monday 23–Friday 27 November 2026
Staff brief: 0 minutes.
Teacher: Hidden staff reference. Use fictional cases and the right to pass. Do not ask pupils to disclose abuse, private messages or family concerns in class. Follow local safeguarding procedures for any real concern. No acted collapse, physical first-aid practice or live emergency call forms part of this lesson.

Purpose and success checks

Safe teaching evidence and learner voice
Boundaries

Use fictional cases and the right to pass. Do not ask pupils to disclose abuse, private messages or family concerns in class. Follow local safeguarding procedures for any real concern. No acted collapse, physical first-aid practice or live emergency call forms part of this lesson.
Assessment and feedback

Task help: ask for the unclear step. Safety concern: tell a trusted adult promptly and privately. Unconscious person: emergency help/999 now. Accept speaking, a note, pointing or AAC. Retain the learner’s request and the real adult reply in the classroom practice, without claiming that a fictional emergency occurred.

Retain actual work, response mode and support. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // (self-edit) · ? (read back) · R (responded) · E (evidence in the school's evidence record). R requires Voice, Audience, an NS+ prompt and the learner’s response in their own colour. Record E only after evidence is banked. Blank forms and adult models are not completed learner evidence.
Lundy moments
Space: calm, accessible participation. Voice: a choice, reason or help request. Audience: the adult listens or reads and replies. Influence: record the support or next-step change made in response.
Speaking listening and writing

Make a clear request, listen to a reply, ask for clarification and record a short next step. The receiving teacher maps authentic responses to their own portfolio; no communication criteria are assigned here.

Staff answers and response guide
Ask for help and keep trying
These are possible responses and task guides, not learner observations. Accept a defensible answer based on the facts or actual work. Record each learner’s reasoning and support.

Model and hinge

Jo is stuck with a task. Jo chooses a trusted staff member. Jo says: Please show me the first step. For a private worry, Jo asks for a quiet talk. If that adult is busy, Jo asks who can help. If someone is in danger, Jo gets help now.

C. Ask another trusted adult, particularly if the need is urgent. For an ordinary task query, agree a short time to return; a danger or safety worry must not wait for an appointment. Rehearse the words “I need help now” or a pointed help card.
Individual evidence key

Task help: ask for the unclear step. Safety concern: tell a trusted adult promptly and privately. Unconscious person: emergency help/999 now. Accept speaking, a note, pointing or AAC. Retain the learner’s request and the real adult reply in the classroom practice, without claiming that a fictional emergency occurred.
Feedback boundaries and next teaching
Card A: A precise request is useful. A short agreed wait can be appropriate for an ordinary task.
Card B: Do not display real messages or ask for personal stories.
Card C: A point, gesture, AAC response or adult-scribed words can be valid; record the mode.
Card D: If danger is immediate, do not wait for the first adult.
Card E: Do not practise a collapse or first-aid technique. In real life call 999, follow instructions and keep yourself safe.
Card F: The learner is not at fault if an adult responds poorly. Staff must use the safeguarding route.
Common misunderstandings

Asking for help is a skill, not a failure. A task question can sometimes wait briefly; immediate danger cannot. One poor response does not mean nobody can help. A friend may support asking, but is not a substitute for an adult or emergency service when needed.
Teaching boundary

Use fictional cases and the right to pass. Do not ask pupils to disclose abuse, private messages or family concerns in class. Follow local safeguarding procedures for any real concern. No acted collapse, physical first-aid practice or live emergency call forms part of this lesson.
Feedback

If a reason is missing, return to the fact or actual work. Re-model a different example, then keep the learner’s own revision. Use NS+ and the learner response in their own colour before R. E means evidence actually banked. Keep safeguarding records separate.
